## ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE.

For Plato believes that vision is formed according to clarity, namely that which flows from the eyes to the external air as one, and that which is brought back from light originating from bodies to meet it. Furthermore, he posits that the vision which exists in the intermediate air is easily diffused and turns, being coextensive with the fire-like faculty of sight. Galen agrees with Plato, but Hipparchus says that rays are extended from the eyes to the bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and that this renders them perceptible to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that the images of things that appear insert themselves into the eyes. Aristotle believes that the images are not themselves bodies, but that they arrive from visible objects to the sight through an alteration of the air which surrounds them. Porphyry, however, considers neither rays nor images, nor anything else, to be the cause of seeing; rather, it is the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible, and being one for all, knowing itself in all things that exist. But the geometers and opticians, leaning somewhat toward Hipparchus, subscribe to certain cones formed from the coincidence of rays, which are emitted through the eyes. From this, they believe that sight comprehends many visible things at once, but those things most accurately where the rays coincide. But indeed, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; the Latinized name of the 9th-century philosopher Al-Kindi</note> teaches something else entirely regarding aspects. To Augustine, it seems that the power of the soul in the eye effects something which has not yet been investigated by scholars of wisdom. Therefore, this science contributes much to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves architecture in measuring buildings. It is closest, however, to the art of painting, and confers great ornament upon the construction of mirrors, such that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it shows by what reasoning we may neither miscount nor shape things in a deformed manner within the images that are perceived on account of intervals and altitudes.

<summary>This page explores various philosophical and scientific theories regarding the nature of vision, including the perspectives of Plato, Galen, Hipparchus, the Epicureans, Aristotle, Porphyry, and Al-Kindi, before concluding with the practical applications of optics in astronomy, architecture, painting, and mirror-making.</summary>
